sourceTitle: Supporting families and professionals to get children reading
author: William Joseph
post: BookTrust’s website had to serve the professionals who get children reading, without losing parents and carers. Audience insight came before layout.
alt: Abstract motion graphic about the BookTrust website redesign. Audience groups are listed as text. There are no photographs of people.

beats.heading: A website for the people who get children reading
beats.caption: BookTrust. A website for the people who get children reading.

beats.label: free books shared with families each year
beats.caption: BookTrust shares over 3 million free books with families each year.

beats.heading: The audience had shifted.
beats.body: Professionals who support families are now the focus.
beats.caption: Professionals who support families are now front and centre.

beats.heading: Who we listened to
beats.caption: We listened to teachers, librarians, health visitors, social workers and early years professionals.

beats.heading: Families still need a front door.
beats.body: A clear path for professionals, and one for parents and carers.
beats.caption: Parents and carers still need a clear path through the same website.

beats.heading: Insight before interface.
beats.body: Research was trauma-informed. People were partners in the work.
beats.caption: Research was trauma-informed. People were partners in the work.

beats.heading: Design from what people need.
beats.caption: Design from what people actually need.

author: Ed Risbey
post: Charity rebrands are not commercial rebrands with a new coat of paint. Spend the money well, meet people where they are, and build a brand the team can actually use.
alt: Motion graphic from William Joseph on why charity rebrands are different, including the share of small and micro charities and four practical tests.

beats.heading: Why charity rebrands are different
beats.caption: Why charity rebrands are different.

beats.heading: You are among peers, not rivals.
beats.body: Partners, patrons and the people you serve come first.
beats.caption: Charities work with peers, partners and patrons.

beats.label: of the sector is small and micro charities
beats.caption: Over 80 percent of the sector is small and micro charities.

beats.heading: Spend the money well.
beats.body: A rebrand should help the mission. If it cannot, pause.
beats.caption: A rebrand should help the mission. If it cannot, pause.

beats.heading: Bold is welcome.
beats.body: Looking wasteful is not. Authentic beats expensive.
beats.caption: Bold is welcome. Looking wasteful is not.

beats.heading: Accessible does not mean ugly.
beats.body: Contrast, type and structure are the brand.
beats.caption: Accessible does not mean ugly. Contrast, type and structure are the brand.

beats.heading: Empower the team.
beats.body: If the team cannot use the brand, it will not last.
beats.caption: If the team cannot use the brand, it will not last.

beats.heading: Root it in mission, people and audiences.
beats.caption: Root the rebrand in mission, people and audiences.

sourceTitle: Digital maturity: the what, why and how
author: Yasmin Georgiou
post: Digital maturity is not a league table. It is how a charity reaches digital goals that are actually tied to the mission. The organisations that describe themselves as digitally mature are far more likely to get there.
alt: Motion graphic defining digital maturity, with figures from the Salesforce Nonprofit Trends report and a now, next and future matrix.

beats.heading: Digital maturity is a practice, not a score
beats.caption: Digital maturity is a practice, not a score.

beats.quote: Reaching digital goals that are linked to organisational goals.
beats.caption: Digital maturity means reaching digital goals linked to organisational goals.

beats.label: of not-for-profits describe themselves as digitally mature
beats.caption: Only 12 percent of not-for-profits describe themselves as digitally mature.

beats.label: more likely to achieve their mission goals
beats.caption: Digitally mature organisations are four times more likely to achieve their mission goals.

beats.heading: Three building blocks
items: A vision of what good looks like
A matrix from now to future
beats.caption: Three building blocks. Categories, a vision of what good looks like, and a matrix.

beats.heading: Plot now, next and future.
beats.body: Levels run from 1 to 5, across the whole organisation.
beats.caption: Plot now, next and future, from level 1 up to the vision.

beats.heading: High numbers can still be fragile.
beats.body: Strong performance can hide an unsustainable culture.
beats.caption: If performance is high and maturity is low, the result may not last.

beats.heading: Make the model fit the organisation.
beats.caption: Make the digital maturity model fit the organisation.

sourceTitle: A refreshed brand and website for a bold new mission, culture and focus on fairness
author: William Joseph
post: Paul Hamlyn Foundation’s brand needed to feel as fair, and as warm, as the relationships behind it. A refreshed identity and a clearer fund finder closed that gap.
alt: Abstract motion graphic about the Paul Hamlyn Foundation brand and website. A simple fund finder is shown. There are no photographs of people.

beats.heading: A brand that feels like the relationship
beats.caption: Paul Hamlyn Foundation. A brand that feels like the relationship.

beats.heading: The identity lagged behind the mission.
beats.body: Warm, long-term relationships were not yet visible.
beats.caption: The old identity lagged behind a mission centred on fairness.

beats.heading: We started with both sides of the table.
beats.body: Grantees and the team shaped a shared mission language.
beats.caption: Grantees and the team shaped a shared language for the mission.

beats.heading: Fund finding, in plain language
beats.caption: Show who the fund is for, the amount, the duration and when to apply.

beats.heading: A finder should remove a barrier.
beats.body: It should never get in the way.
beats.caption: A fund finder should remove a barrier, not add one.

beats.heading: Built to be used, not only admired.
beats.body: A toolkit the team can carry, on a site applicants can follow.
beats.caption: A visual toolkit the team can use, and a site applicants can follow.

beats.heading: Bold and colourful. Highly accessible.
beats.caption: Bold and colourful, and highly accessible.

sourceTitle: Investigating public attitudes to artificial intelligence
author: William Joseph
post: The British public is not simply for or against AI. A nationally representative survey shows where people feel the benefit, and where they want a human in the loop.
alt: Motion graphic of survey findings on public attitudes to AI in Britain, including cancer detection and concern about professional judgement. No photographs of people.

beats.heading: What the public actually thinks about AI
beats.caption: What the public actually thinks about AI.

beats.label: adults in Britain took part in the survey
beats.source: Ada Lovelace Institute and the Alan Turing Institute
beats.caption: More than 4,000 adults in Britain took part in a nationally representative survey.

beats.heading: People are broadly positive.
beats.body: They are also highly specific. The use matters more than the label.
beats.caption: People are broadly positive about AI, and highly specific about each use.

beats.label: find AI for cancer detection broadly beneficial
beats.source: Ada Lovelace Institute and the Alan Turing Institute
beats.caption: 9 in 10 adults find AI for cancer detection broadly beneficial.

beats.label: worry about replacing professional judgement
beats.source: Ada Lovelace Institute and the Alan Turing Institute
beats.caption: 56 percent worry about relying on the technology instead of professional judgement.

beats.heading: People want regulation.
beats.body: That view is not the same in every age group.
beats.caption: People want AI regulation, and that view changes with age.

beats.heading: Design for nuance, not a single opinion.
beats.caption: Design for nuance, not a single public opinion.

sourceTitle: Seven barriers to creating a content-led culture and how to overcome them
author: Yasmin Georgiou
post: A content strategy only sticks when the culture does. Seven barriers we see in almost every charity, and a practical way through each one.
alt: Motion graphic from William Joseph. A title for seven barriers to a content-led culture, a diagram of people, processes and tools, then one action for each barrier.

beats.heading: Seven barriers to creating a content-led culture
beats.caption: Seven barriers to creating a content-led culture.

beats.heading: A strategy only sticks when the culture does.
beats.body: Move people, processes and tools together.
beats.caption: A strategy only sticks when the culture does.

beats.heading: Content culture lives in the overlap
beats.caption: Content culture sits where people, processes and tools overlap.

beats.heading: Shared understanding
beats.body: Co-create what content means for your organisation.
beats.caption: 1 of 7. Shared understanding. Co-create what content means for you.

beats.heading: Relationships
beats.body: Group people by what they need, not by job title.
beats.caption: 2 of 7. Relationships. Group people by what they need.

beats.heading: Common goals
beats.body: Name what you share, and where you truly differ.
beats.caption: 3 of 7. Common goals. Name what you share and where you differ.

beats.heading: Ways of working
beats.body: Design the process while you write the strategy.
beats.caption: 4 of 7. Ways of working. Design the process while you write the strategy.

beats.heading: Skills and capabilities
beats.body: Make time to practise, not only to read.
beats.caption: 5 of 7. Skills and capabilities. Make time to practise, not only to read.

beats.heading: Audience insight
beats.body: Start small, then let the evidence make the case.
beats.caption: 6 of 7. Audience insight. Start small, then let evidence make the case.

beats.heading: Measurement
beats.body: Set goals everyone can see, and talk about them often.
beats.caption: 7 of 7. Measurement. Set goals everyone can see, and talk about them.

beats.heading: Start with one honest conversation.
beats.caption: Start with one honest conversation. William Joseph.
